reference.one_line: 46-year-old man with NPM1-mutated acute myeloid leukaemia, induction day 13, neutropenic fever since 16 Nov from a probable central line infection; platelets 8, vancomycin about to start.

handoff.summary: Tobiah Quenneville, 46, is on day 13 of induction for acute myeloid leukaemia with neutrophils 0.0, haemoglobin 7.6 g/dL and platelets 8. He has been febrile since 02:00 on 16 Nov (38.3 at 14:00 today, heart rate 110, blood pressure 109/63, room air) on cefepime. The red-lumen blood culture grew gram-positive cocci in clusters at 31 hours and the line exit site has 1 cm of tender redness; infectious diseases advises vancomycin, first dose due 14:30, with the line kept for now. Platelets planned for this morning have not been given despite gum bleeding and a nosebleed at 09:50. A bisacodyl suppository order is active against the nothing-by-rectum precaution.
to_do: Start vancomycin 1,250 mg at 14:30 through the white lumen over 90 minutes; rotate lumens with later doses
Transfuse 1 unit of irradiated, leucocyte-reduced platelets now (count 8 with fever and bleeding)
Get the bisacodyl suppository cancelled and an oral laxative ordered (no bowel movement since 13 Nov)
Chase the rapid Staphylococcus aureus result and the repeat cultures drawn at 10:30
Ask about magnesium replacement (1.6 mg/dL) and a potassium recheck; QTc 438 ms on posaconazole and ondansetron
Cefepime due 20:00; temperature before every acetaminophen dose
if_then: If systolic pressure falls below 90, heart rate exceeds 130 or he becomes confused, then call the rapid response team and the resident and check lactate
If the laboratory reports Staphylococcus aureus, the tunnel becomes tender or pus appears, then call the team about removing the line
If he has a headache, visual change, black stools or bleeding that does not stop in 10 minutes, then call the resident at once and recheck the platelet count
If he reacts to vancomycin with flushing or itching, then slow the infusion and call the resident

reference.brief_hospital_course: Mr Quenneville is a 46-year-old teacher admitted on 2 Nov from the haematology urgent clinic with white cells of 46.2 and 62% blasts after six weeks of fatigue, bruising and bleeding gums. Bone marrow biopsy on 3 Nov showed acute myeloid leukaemia with mutated NPM1, a normal karyotype and no FLT3 mutation (favourable risk). Tumour lysis risk was managed with fluids and allopurinol and did not develop. An echocardiogram was normal and a tunnelled double-lumen line was placed on 4 Nov. Induction with cytarabine for 7 days and daunorubicin for 3 days ran from 5 to 12 Nov on posaconazole, acyclovir and levofloxacin prophylaxis. He became pancytopenic and transfusion dependent, with mouth ulcers managed with rinses and oxycodone. Redness at the line exit site was first charted on the evening of 15 Nov. At 02:00 on 16 Nov he had a fever of 38.4 with rigors; cultures were drawn at 02:25 and cefepime was started at 04:35, delayed because it had to come from central pharmacy. Fever has continued. CT chest on 17 Nov was clear. The red-lumen culture grew gram-positive cocci in clusters at 31 hours, with the other sets negative so far; infectious diseases considers a catheter-related infection most likely, and vancomycin starts today with the line kept for now. On day 13 neutrophils are 0.0, haemoglobin 7.6 g/dL and platelets 8, with gum bleeding and a nosebleed; the platelet transfusion planned this morning has not yet been given.

Probable catheter-related bloodstream infection: red-lumen culture gram-positive cocci in clusters, exit site 1 cm tender redness

Mouth ulcers from chemotherapy, pain 4 to 5 out of 10
Low potassium 3.4 mmol/L and magnesium 1.6 mg/dL on QT-prolonging medicines
Opioid-related constipation, no bowel movement since 13 Nov

Nothing by rectum with neutrophils 0.0 and platelets 8; use an oral laxative.
Not enough alone; add an oral osmotic laxative.
Given 09:20; pharmacy targets potassium above 4.0 and magnesium above 2.0 and suggests intravenous magnesium 2 g, not yet ordered.
QTc 438 ms acceptable; keep electrolytes replaced.

Must not be restarted with low platelets.

Vancomycin first dose 14:30; level before the fourth dose

qa.q: What type of leukaemia does he have and what is the risk group?
qa.a: Acute myeloid leukaemia with mutated NPM1, normal karyotype (46,XY), FLT3 not mutated: favourable genetic risk.
evidence: path: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy

qa.q: What vancomycin dose is ordered and on what basis?
qa.a: 1,250 mg every 12 hours, 15 mg/kg at 83.4 kg with creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (clearance above 100 mL/min); first dose due 14:30, level before the fourth dose.
438 ms on 16 Nov, against 431 ms on 4 Nov before posaconazole.
1.4 on 2 Nov, 0.3 on 11 Nov, 0.04 on 14 Nov, and 0.0 on 16 and 17 Nov.

qa.q: What have his platelets done over the last four days?
qa.a: 9 on 14 Nov, 14 on 16 Nov (one unit given at 07:10), 8 on 17 Nov at 05:10.

qa.q: Are the infection markers improving on cefepime?
qa.a: No. C-reactive protein rose from 86 to 142 mg/L and procalcitonin from 0.4 to 0.9 ng/mL; lactate is normal at 1.2 mmol/L.

qa.q: How long after the first fever was the first antibiotic given?
qa.a: 2 hours 35 minutes: 38.4 at 02:00 on 16 Nov, cefepime at 04:35. The target is 60 minutes.

qa.q: When was a change at the line exit site first charted?
qa.a: At the dressing change at 17:50 on 15 Nov (faint redness, 5 mm), about 8 hours before the first fever. It was 1 cm and tender by the evening of 16 Nov.

qa.q: When did the blood culture turn positive, and from which sample?
qa.a: The aerobic bottle from the red lumen flagged at 09:40 on 17 Nov, 31 hours after collection, and was phoned to the nurse at 09:55. White-lumen and peripheral sets show no growth at 36 hours.

qa.q: Is a platelet transfusion indicated, and has it been given?
qa.a: Yes: 8 is below both thresholds (under 10; under 20 with fever or bleeding). None is charted today and intake shows no blood products.
evidence: flowsheet: Transfusions given; Intake and output

qa.q: Should the central line be removed now?
qa.a: Not yet, per infectious diseases. Remove it if Staphylococcus aureus is identified, the tunnel becomes tender, he becomes unstable or cultures stay positive after 72 hours of vancomycin.

qa.q: Which organism grew, and is it methicillin resistant?
qa.a: Not yet known. The chart has only the Gram stain (gram-positive cocci in clusters); identification, susceptibility and the rapid test are in progress.

qa.q: Has he been screened for MRSA carriage?
qa.a: No screening swab or result is recorded.

epilogue.note: What happens AFTER 'now' in this simulated world. Never shown in the chart; for outcome-prediction ground truth.
epilogue.course: Vancomycin started at 14:40. The day nurse caught the suppository order and it was replaced with polyethylene glycol. The missed platelets surfaced only when a second nosebleed lasted 25 minutes; a unit was given at 17:40. At 18:05 the rapid test reported methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, which cefepime had not covered. That night he had a rigor with a blood pressure of 84/46 and lactate of 3.4, received 2.5 L of fluid and spent about a day and a half in intensive care on low-dose noradrenaline. The line was removed on 18 Nov. Cultures cleared on 19 Nov, an echocardiogram showed no valve infection and the fever settled by 21 Nov; creatinine peaked at 1.5 mg/dL. Neutrophils recovered on 30 Nov and the marrow on 2 Dec showed remission. He went home on 4 Dec with home vancomycin until 17 Dec. One emergency visit for a fever on 7 Dec proved to be a cold. Consolidation started two weeks late.

events.event: First vancomycin dose started through the white lumen
Bisacodyl suppository cancelled after the day nurse raised it; polyethylene glycol 17 g daily ordered
Platelets transfused after a second, 25-minute nosebleed at 16:15; count afterwards 26
Rapid test: Staphylococcus aureus, methicillin resistant
Rigor, temperature 39.2, blood pressure 84/46, lactate 3.4; rapid response, 2.5 L fluid
Transferred to intensive care; noradrenaline for 11 hours
Tunnelled line removed after a further platelet unit; tip later grew the same organism
Back on 7 South; first negative blood cultures drawn this morning
Arm line placed for antibiotics after a week of negative cultures
Discharged home with home infusion nursing for vancomycin until 17 Dec

outcomes_30_day.notable: In remission; first consolidation cycle began as a planned admission on 21 Dec, two weeks later than intended.

portal_messages.subject: Gums still bleeding and now bruises
portal_messages.body: Hello, I saw the dentist two weeks ago about bleeding gums and she said to get checked if the mouthwash didn't sort it. It hasn't. I've also got bruises on my arms and shins that I can't account for, and I'm out of breath on the school stairs, which isn't like me. I've been tired since September and taking ibuprofen for headaches. Probably just run down, but should I book something or give it more time?
ideal_reply_points: Bleeding gums, unexplained bruising, fatigue and breathlessness together need an examination and blood count today or tomorrow, not in a few weeks
Go to the emergency department for heavy bleeding, fever, black stools or severe headache

portal_messages.subject: Re: Gums still bleeding and now bruises
portal_messages.body: Good morning Mr Quenneville. Thank you for writing; please don't wait on this. The doctor would like to see you and take blood tests. I have booked you for tomorrow, Friday 30 October, at 3:40 pm. Please stop the ibuprofen from today, as it can make bleeding worse; acetaminophen is fine for headaches. If you have a nosebleed that won't stop, black stools, a fever or a severe headache before then, go to the emergency department.

portal_messages.subject: Visiting, and what I can bring in
portal_messages.body: This is Marisol, Tobiah's wife. His sister flies in on Friday and wants to come straight from the airport. Is that all right now he has a fever? She's had her flu jab. Also, he's barely eating with his mouth so sore. Can I bring soup from home, and his own pillow? The children have made cards and want to send flowers; I wasn't sure about those. Thank you all for last night.
ideal_reply_points: Sister may visit if she is well, cleans her hands and wears a mask if she has any symptoms after travelling
No fresh flowers or plants; cards are welcome
Home food must be freshly and thoroughly cooked and eaten hot; nothing raw or unpasteurised
A freshly laundered pillow is fine; offer the family support programme for the children

portal_messages.subject: Temperature 38.1 tonight
portal_messages.body: Home since Friday. This evening I've got a temperature of 38.1 and feel shivery. The nurse did my vancomycin through the arm line at four and it all looked fine, no redness. My daughter's had a streaming cold all week so I expect it's that. I'm in clinic on Wednesday anyway. Is it OK to take acetaminophen and wait until then?
ideal_reply_points: No: a temperature of 38.0 or more after chemotherapy with a line in place means come to the emergency department now
Do not take acetaminophen first; it hides the fever
He needs blood cultures and a blood count tonight even if it turns out to be a cold
Bring the fever card and say he has had a line infection

portal_messages.subject: Re: Temperature 38.1 tonight
portal_messages.body: Tobiah, I have also left you a voicemail. Please do not wait for Wednesday. With a temperature of 38.1, your recent treatment and a line in your arm, you need to come to the emergency department now. Do not take acetaminophen before you are seen. I have told them to expect you and to take blood cultures from the line and your arm. It may well be your daughter's cold, but we have to be sure. Ask Marisol to drive.
ideal_reply_points: Warm handover to the emergency department

conversation.setting: Bedside in 7S-03, 17 Nov at about 11:15: infectious diseases consult

turns.speaker: Dr. Lindholm-Reyes
turns.text: Mr Quenneville? I'm Dr Lindholm-Reyes from the infection team. Your haematology doctors asked me to come because the fevers are carrying on. All right if I ask a few questions and take a look?

turns.speaker: Tobiah
turns.text: Sure. Tobiah's fine. Excuse the mumbling, my mouth's in ribbons.

turns.speaker: Dr. Lindholm-Reyes
turns.text: I'll keep it short. The first fever was the early hours of yesterday?

turns.speaker: Tobiah
turns.text: About two in the morning. I woke up shaking, proper teeth-chattering. Though honestly I felt cold the evening before. Around ten I told the nurse I was chilly.

turns.speaker: Dr. Lindholm-Reyes
turns.text: That's useful. And since?

turns.speaker: Tobiah
turns.text: Up and down. Shook again last night, about half one.

turns.speaker: Dr. Lindholm-Reyes
turns.text: You were 38.6 at two and 37.9 at ten this morning. Any cough? Short of breath?

turns.speaker: Tobiah
turns.text: No. They scanned my chest first thing.

turns.speaker: Dr. Lindholm-Reyes
turns.text: And it's clear, which is good news: no pneumonia and nothing to suggest a fungal infection. Tummy pain? Diarrhoea?

turns.speaker: Tobiah
turns.text: Opposite problem. Nothing since Friday.

turns.speaker: Dr. Lindholm-Reyes
turns.text: Any pain around your back passage, when you sit or...

turns.speaker: Tobiah
turns.text: No, nothing like that. The night nurse did say there's a suppository written up if I want it.

turns.speaker: Dr. Lindholm-Reyes
turns.text: Please don't have that. With no white cells and platelets this low, nothing goes in by the back passage. It can cause bleeding and let gut bacteria into the blood. I'll put that in my advice to the team; there are things you can drink instead.

turns.speaker: Tobiah
turns.text: Fine by me.

turns.speaker: Dr. Lindholm-Reyes
turns.text: Let me look at your mouth. As wide as is comfortable... ulcers on both cheeks. I'm going to scrape gently. That doesn't lift off, so it isn't thrush. Chest is clear. Tummy's soft. Does it hurt when I press?

turns.speaker: Tobiah
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Dr. Lindholm-Reyes
turns.text: I'll just look at your bottom from the outside; I won't examine inside. That's fine. Now the line. When did anyone first notice anything there?

turns.speaker: Tobiah
turns.text: When they changed the dressing Sunday teatime, the nurse said it was a bit pink. Didn't hurt then. It does now if you press it.

turns.speaker: Dr. Lindholm-Reyes
turns.text: About a centimetre of redness, and yes, tender just there. No pus. And along here, where it runs under the skin?

turns.speaker: Tobiah
turns.text: No, that's fine.

turns.speaker: Dr. Lindholm-Reyes
turns.text: Good. Here's what I think. One of the blood samples from yesterday morning, the one taken through the red side of the line, has started growing bacteria. Under the microscope they look like the staph family, bugs that live on skin. The white side and the sample from your arm haven't grown anything so far.

turns.speaker: Tobiah
turns.text: So the line's infected. The thing that's meant to be helping me.

turns.speaker: Dr. Lindholm-Reyes
turns.text: Most likely. One bottle on its own can be a skin bug that got in when the sample was taken, but with the site going red before the fever I think it's real. So I'm recommending a second antibiotic today, vancomycin, on top of the one you're on.

turns.speaker: Tobiah
turns.text: Does the line have to come out?

turns.speaker: Dr. Lindholm-Reyes
turns.text: Not yet. It comes out if the lab names it as Staph aureus, the more aggressive one, or if that track under the skin gets sore, or you become unwell with your blood pressure, or the blood is still growing it after three days of vancomycin.

turns.speaker: Tobiah
turns.text: And if it isn't the line?

turns.speaker: Dr. Lindholm-Reyes
turns.text: Then we keep looking. We're sending a blood test for fungal infection, and if you're still having fevers in a few days with nothing growing we'd think again about antifungal treatment. Your antifungal and antiviral tablets carry on.

turns.speaker: Tobiah
turns.text: Let me check I've got it. Bug in the red tube, probably off the skin. Second antibiotic today. Line stays unless it's the nasty staph or I get worse.

turns.speaker: Dr. Lindholm-Reyes
turns.text: Exactly right. More blood cultures were taken at half ten, and we repeat them every day until they're clean. And nothing by the back passage.

turns.speaker: Tobiah
turns.text: Got it. Thanks for explaining it properly.

turns.speaker: Dr. Lindholm-Reyes
turns.text: I'll see you tomorrow.
